stories.headline: Democrats win Congress: what they can and cannot do to Trump
stories.question: Democrats now control both houses of Congress. What can they actually do to Trump?
stories.dek: They can block his bills, investigate his officials and stall his nominees. To override his veto or remove him, they need two-thirds votes. A simple majority does not give them that.

so_far.text: The US Congress has two chambers, the House of Representatives and the Senate. A bill must pass both before it goes to the President. Midterm elections fall halfway through a President's four-year term. This year they were held on 3 November 2026. Before the vote, Republicans held the Senate 53 to 47. Democrats needed a net gain of four seats for a 51-seat majority. A 50-50 tie would go to Republicans, because Vice President JD Vance breaks ties. Voters said living costs, tariffs and the Iran war mattered to them. The Iran war had raised fuel prices.

what_happened.text: On 4 November 2026, AP and other outlets reported that Democrats had won control of both the House and the Senate. Democrats flipped Senate seats in Kansas, Texas and North Carolina. They won in Ohio and South Carolina, and held Michigan, Georgia and New Hampshire. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat to win a Senate race there since 1932. Final seat totals were not yet reported. Trump said he was 'absolutely willing to accept those results' and would 'work with the Democrats'. Minutes later he posted a picture of a red 'VETO' cap.

steps.text: A bill becomes law only if both houses pass it, so Democrats can now stop any Trump bill.
But Trump can veto any bill they pass, and overriding a veto needs two-thirds of both houses.
Some powers need no presidential signature: committees can investigate, and the Senate can reject judges and senior officials.
Congress also controls spending, so Democrats can scrutinise defence budgets and constrain Iran and Ukraine policy.
The House can impeach by simple majority, but removal needs two-thirds of the Senate, which means Republican votes.

lesson.concept: Why a majority can block, but not overrule, a President
lesson.big_idea: A simple majority in Congress lets a party stop bills, investigate and reject nominees. Overriding a veto, or removing a President, needs two-thirds votes. So it needs help from the other party.

steps.title: Bills need both houses
steps.text: A bill must pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate. In the final vote in each house, a simple majority is enough. A simple majority means more than half of those voting.

steps.title: The President can veto
steps.text: Next, the President signs the bill or vetoes it. A veto means he refuses to sign. A vetoed bill dies. Trump keeps this power even with a Democratic Congress.

steps.title: Override needs two-thirds
steps.text: Congress can overturn a veto only if two-thirds of those voting in BOTH houses agree. The Senate has 100 seats. If every senator votes, two-thirds means 67 senators.

steps.title: Powers that need no signature
steps.text: Some powers belong to Congress alone. Committees can investigate the government. The Senate can reject judges and senior officials. Congress can scrutinise spending, including on defence. A majority is enough for all of these.

steps.title: Impeach by majority, remove by two-thirds
steps.text: The House can impeach a President by simple majority. Impeach means formally charge. The Senate then holds a trial. To remove him, two-thirds of senators must vote guilty. That is 67 if all 100 vote.

example.setup: Imagine a 100-seat Senate where Party A holds 52 seats and Party B holds 48. Party A also controls the House. Assume all 100 senators vote every time.

lines.label: Majority needed
lines.note: Party A's 52 seats can pass bills.

lines.label: President vetoes
lines.note: Unless Congress overrides the veto.

lines.label: Override target
lines.note: You cannot have part of a senator.

lines.label: Votes short
lines.note: Party A needs 15 senators from Party B.

lines.label: Removal after impeachment
lines.note: Same two-thirds bar, same 15-vote gap.

example.result: Party A's 52 seats let it pass bills, block bills and investigate. To beat a veto or remove a President, it must win over 15 senators from the other party.

apply.text: On 4 November 2026, outlets projected that Democrats had won both houses. Before the vote they held 47 Senate seats, far short of two-thirds. Final totals are not yet known. Like Party A, they can block Trump's bills, investigate and stall nominees. His veto stands unless Republicans join them. Removal after any impeachment, which Ted Cruz predicts, would also need Republican votes.

practice.q: Suppose Party A holds 55 of 100 Senate seats and the President vetoes its bill. How many Party B senators must join to override?
practice.answer: Two-thirds of 100 is 66.7, so round up to 67. Party A has 55. 67 − 55 = 12. Party A needs 12 senators from Party B. It also needs two-thirds of the House.

check.why: A majority can pass a bill, but only two-thirds of both houses can override a veto. That needs Republican votes.

scenes.show: What can Congress do to Trump?

scenes.say: On the fourth of November, news agencies reported that Democrats had won both the House and the Senate. They even took Senate seats in Kansas and Texas.
Before the vote, Republicans held the Senate fifty-three to forty-seven. Democrats needed a net gain of four seats.

Here is the key idea. Imagine a Senate of one hundred, where your party holds fifty-two seats. Fifty-one is a majority, so you can pass bills. But the President can veto them. To override, you need two-thirds. That is sixty-seven senators. Sixty-seven minus fifty-two leaves you fifteen votes short.
But a majority can do some things alone. It can investigate the government, reject judges and senior officials, and scrutinise defence spending.
That is why Trump, minutes after saying he accepts the results, posted a picture of a red veto cap. And impeachment, which Senator Ted Cruz predicts, would still need Republican votes to remove him.
Remember this. A majority can block, but only two-thirds can overrule. The new Congress is sworn in during the first week of January twenty twenty-seven.

stories.headline: Trump says US aid to Israel ends this year. Can he?
stories.question: Is the US really ending its $3.8 billion a year in military aid to Israel?
stories.dek: Not yet. Trump announced it in a TV interview, but no order has been reported. Under US law, Congress controls this money, not the president alone.

so_far.text: In 2016 the US and Israel signed a ten-year agreement called a memorandum of understanding (MOU). It covers fiscal years 2019 to 2028 and promises $38 billion. That is about $3.3 billion a year to buy weapons, plus $500 million a year for missile defence, or roughly $3.8 billion a year. In an interview in May, Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he wanted to 'taper off American support for Israel to zero'. He has long preferred a slow phase-out over about a decade. Earlier in 2026, Republican congressman Marlin Stutzman proposed a non-binding resolution to replace the MOU and end the aid.

what_happened.text: On 3 November 2026, President Donald Trump told Fox News that he and Netanyahu 'made a deal months ago that we're stopping'. He said that by the end of this year 'we won't be paying Israel'. He said Netanyahu 'brought it up' and that Israel does not need the aid. He also said he did not want to give Democrats a 'talking point' against Republicans. Trump said Israel can still buy US weapons. Asked whether he meant equipment or money, he did not say. No formal order has been reported. Netanyahu's office did not comment.

steps.text: The 2016 MOU is a written promise between two governments, and MOUs are not legally binding on their own.
But Congress, the US parliament, wrote the yearly weapons-aid level into a 2021 defence law.
Real money flows only when Congress passes yearly funding laws, called appropriations.
So a president's spoken deal cannot, by itself, cancel money that Congress has already approved.
That is why the Jerusalem Post notes Congress may need to act, and no congressional reaction has been reported.

lesson.concept: Who really controls US military aid to Israel
lesson.big_idea: Leaders can promise aid, but in the US, Congress writes it into law and releases the money each year. Most of the money is spent back in America, so a clean stop needs Congress.

steps.title: The MOU is a promise
steps.text: In 2016 the US and Israel signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU), a written promise between governments. It covers fiscal years 2019 to 2028: $38 billion over ten years. MOUs are not legally binding on their own.

steps.title: Congress turns it into law
steps.text: Congress, the US parliament, wrote the yearly Foreign Military Financing (FMF) level into a 2021 defence law. FMF is US money given to Israel to buy weapons, about $3.3 billion a year.

steps.title: Money needs yearly approval
steps.text: Each year Congress must also pass appropriations, the laws that release actual money. So a president's understanding alone would not cancel funds Congress has already approved.

steps.title: Most of it is spent in America
steps.text: Israel must spend 92% of its FMF on US-made products in 2026 and 2027, and 100% in 2028. So most of the aid flows back to American companies.

example.setup: Imagine a country, call it Country A, gets an assumed $1 billion a year in US weapons aid. Assume it must spend 90% of that on US-made products.

lines.label: Spent in America
lines.note: This money goes to US arms makers.

lines.label: Spent elsewhere
lines.note: The small share allowed outside the US.

lines.label: Aid stops, buying continues
lines.calc: Country A now pays $900 million itself
lines.note: Arms sales go on; the buyer pays instead of US taxpayers.

lines.label: Who can stop it?
lines.calc: Congress, by changing the law or yearly funding
lines.note: A leader's spoken deal alone is not enough.

example.result: Ending aid does not end the weapons trade. It moves the bill from US taxpayers to the buyer. And because Congress controls the money, a clean stop needs Congress.

apply.text: Now the news. Israel gets about $3.3 billion a year in FMF and must spend 92% of it on US-made goods in 2026, roughly $3 billion. Trump says Israel can still buy US weapons, so ending aid would mainly shift that bill to Israel. But the levels are in a 2021 law and funded yearly by Congress. A formal order? None has been reported.

practice.q: Say Country B gets $2 billion a year and, like Israel in 2028, must spend 100% on US-made products. How much can it spend outside the US?
practice.answer: Spent in America: 100% of $2 billion = $2 billion. Spent elsewhere: $2 billion − $2 billion = $0. Every dollar of the aid goes back to US companies.

stories.headline: Oil falls nearly 9% after Vance blames Iran war for losses
stories.question: Why did oil prices drop so fast while the US and Iran still exchange fire?
stories.dek: Traders are betting the war is closer to ending, not that oil is flowing again. US election losses raised pressure on Trump to make a deal, so the "war premium" in prices shrank.

so_far.text: The US and Iran are at war, and ships in the Gulf are under attack. Iran says the Strait of Hormuz, the sea lane Gulf tankers use, reopens only if the US meets its seven conditions. In October a record 30 attacks hit commercial ships, and Gulf oil exports fell. On 30 October Brent crude was near $118 a barrel. On 2 November the US struck Qeshm Island, and Brent fell to $105.03 on hopes of a deal.

what_happened.text: On 4 November Brent crude, the main world oil price, fell 8.6% to $94.66 a barrel, its lowest since 4 September. WTI, the US price, fell 8.3% to $88.08. So only US oil is below $90. The fall followed US politics. Democrats won control of Congress in the 3 November midterms. Vice President JD Vance wrote on X that the Iran war was the reason for the Republican losses. Markets read this as pressure on Trump to reach a deal. Trump told the Financial Times the US has no immediate plans to strike Iran, but left more action open.

steps.text: An oil price reflects the current supply of barrels plus traders' fear of losing more barrels later.
Through October that fear was high: a record 30 attacks on ships, and Gulf exports falling.
The Democrats' win and Vance's post made a Trump deal with Iran look more likely to traders.
Better odds of a deal shrink the fear part of the price, so Brent fell from near $118 to $94.66.
But barrels have not returned: ships are still attacked, and Iran says Hormuz reopens only on its terms.

lesson.concept: How a war risk premium moves oil prices
lesson.big_idea: An oil price has two parts: what barrels are worth with current supply, plus extra for the fear of losing more supply. When fear falls, prices fall, even before more oil flows.

steps.title: Start with the calm price
steps.text: Imagine there is no threat at all. The price then depends only on how much oil is pumped and how much the world wants. Call this the calm price.

steps.title: Add a disaster price
steps.text: If a key route like the Strait of Hormuz shut fully, oil would be scarce and buyers would pay much more. The gap between the two prices is the extra cost of disaster.

steps.title: Weigh it by the odds
steps.text: Traders don't know if disaster will come. So they pay the calm price plus the extra cost times their chance of disaster. That added piece is the risk premium.

steps.title: News changes the odds
steps.text: News that makes peace look likelier lowers the chance, so the premium shrinks. On 4 November markets read Vance's post as pressure on Trump to reach a deal.

steps.title: Real barrels still set a floor
steps.text: Fear can fade fast, but missing barrels keep prices up. Gulf exports were 17.1 million barrels a day in October, about three-quarters of pre-war levels.

example.setup: Imagine traders think oil is worth $80 a barrel in calm times and $130 if Hormuz shuts completely. All these numbers are made up. Watch what happens when their fear changes.

lines.label: Extra cost of disaster
lines.note: How much worse a full shutdown would be

lines.label: Before: 60% chance
lines.note: Fear is high after weeks of ship attacks

lines.label: Price before
lines.note: Calm price plus the fear part

lines.label: After: 30% chance
lines.note: Election news makes a deal look likelier

lines.label: Price after
lines.note: No new barrels, yet the price falls $15

example.result: Halving the fear cut the price by $15 without one extra barrel moving. Brent's real fall, from $105.03 on 2 November to $94.66 on 4 November, has a similar shape.

apply.text: On 4 November the sea did not get safer: a tanker was hit off Oman on 3 November and Gulf exports were down. What changed was the odds. Democrats won Congress, Vance blamed the war, and Trump said he had no immediate strike plans. Traders cut the risk premium, so Brent fell 8.6% to $94.66. A new strike could raise the premium just as fast.

practice.q: Same calm price of $80 and disaster price of $130. A new strike pushes traders' chance of disaster to 50%. What is the oil price now?
practice.answer: Extra cost of disaster: $130 − $80 = $50. Premium: 50% of $50 = $25. Price: $80 + $25 = $105. Fear rose, so the price rose $10 from $95, with no change in barrels.

Remember: oil trades on fear, not just barrels. Watch Qatar's mediation around fifth November. A new strike could bring the fear back.

stories.headline: Three in four Agniveers get two more years in uniform
stories.question: What changes for Agniveers now that 75% get a two-year extension?
stories.dek: Most Agniveers will serve six years instead of four. After that, they can be considered for a permanent armed forces post. The selection rules, pay and exit details have not been announced.

so_far.text: Agnipath is a scheme that recruits people into the armed forces on short contracts. The recruits are called Agniveers. The scheme began on 14 June 2022. Each Agniveer served four years. After that, 25% could join the regular forces on merit, and the rest left service. The scheme was criticised over the short tenure and the future of the 75% who were not kept. Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Maharashtra announced reservations for ex-Agniveers in police and government jobs.

what_happened.text: On 4 November 2026 the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), Gen NS Raja Subramani, announced a change to Agnipath. The Cabinet had approved it. 75% of Agniveers will get a two-year extension beyond their four-year tenure. After those two extra years, they can be considered for regular enrolment through objective selection. This replaces the old arrangement, under which only 25% were eligible. The CDS did not give details of the selection criteria. The decision comes as the first batch nears the end of its four years.

steps.text: Under the old rule, three in four Agniveers left after four years, which raised worries about their futures.
The first batch is now close to finishing four years, so a decision on their future was due.
The CDS said the forces assessed that batch's performance and got very positive feedback.
So the Cabinet approved two more years for 75%, then a route to regular enrolment through objective selection.
But permanent posts still depend on objective selection criteria that have not yet been made public.

analogy.text: Think of a long paid internship. Earlier, interns worked four years, and one in four could stay on in a permanent job. Now three in four get two extra years. After that, they can be considered for a permanent job through a test. The test decides who stays.
analogy.breaks: Unlike a company internship, the test rules and the number of permanent posts have not been made public yet.

items.holder: Gen NS Raja Subramani, Chief of Defence Staff

for_you.text: If someone in your family is an Agniveer, they have a three-in-four chance of getting six years of service, not four. After that, they can be considered for a permanent post through objective selection. Young people weighing the scheme now face a longer path. Pay and benefits for the extra years have not been reported. It is not yet known how this affects state job quotas for ex-Agniveers.

misconception.myth: All extended Agniveers will now become permanent soldiers.
misconception.fact: 75% get two more years. After that they can only be considered for regular enrolment through objective selection, and the criteria have not been given.

lesson.concept: How Agnipath's two gates decide who stays
lesson.big_idea: Agnipath works like a funnel with two gates. The first gate decides what share of recruits moves past the fixed contract. The second gate, selection, decides who becomes a permanent soldier.

steps.title: Everyone starts on a contract
steps.text: Recruits join as Agniveers on a fixed four-year tenure, which means a contract with a set end date. The scheme began on 14 June 2022.

steps.title: The old gate: 25%
steps.text: Under the original scheme, at the end of four years, 25% of Agniveers could join the regular armed forces on merit. The rest left service.

steps.title: The new first gate: 75%
steps.text: Under the revision announced on 4 November 2026, 75% of Agniveers get two extra years. So they serve six years in total.

steps.title: The second gate: selection
steps.text: After those six years, extended Agniveers can be considered for regular enrolment through objective selection, meaning fixed, measurable criteria. Being considered is not the same as being selected. The criteria have not been given.

example.setup: Imagine a batch of 1,000 Agniveers joins on the same day. Let us walk them through the old rule and then the new rule.

lines.label: Old rule: joined regulars
lines.note: They could join the regular forces on merit.

lines.label: Old rule: left
lines.note: Three in four left after four years.

lines.label: New rule: extended
lines.note: This is the new first gate.

lines.label: Their total service
lines.note: Two years longer than the original contract.

lines.label: Second gate
lines.calc: 750 can be considered; number selected unknown
lines.note: Objective selection decides; criteria not yet given.

lines.label: New rule: not extended
lines.note: Sources do not say what happens to them.

example.result: Under the old rule, 250 of 1,000 could join the regular forces after four years. Under the new rule, 750 serve six years and can then be considered. How many become regulars is not yet known.

apply.text: So the CDS's announcement on 4 November 2026 changes the first gate: 75% of Agniveers get two more years. After that, they can be considered for regular enrolment through objective selection. This replaces the old arrangement, where only 25% were eligible. How many get through the second gate depends on criteria that have not yet been given.

practice.q: Imagine a batch of 2,000 Agniveers. How many could join the regular forces under the old rule, and how many get the extension now?
practice.answer: Old rule: 25% of 2,000 = 500 could join on merit, and 2,000 − 500 = 1,500 left. New rule: 75% of 2,000 = 1,500 get two more years, or six in total. They can then be considered for regular enrolment. How many are selected depends on criteria not yet given.

check.q: What does the two-year extension actually give an extended Agniveer?
options: A guaranteed permanent post in the regular armed forces
Two more years of service, then a chance to be considered for regular enrolment
Nothing new, because the 25% rule still decides everything
check.why: The extension adds service time. A permanent post still depends on objective selection, and those criteria have not been published.

takeaways: Agnipath is a funnel: a percentage cut-off, then selection, decides who gets a permanent post.
On 4 November 2026, the CDS announced two extra years for 75% of Agniveers, then possible regular enrolment.
Watch for the selection criteria, pay for the extra years, and the first batch's exit.

stories.headline: AI's hunger for memory chips is pushing up phone and laptop prices
stories.question: Why are memory chip prices soaring, and will phones and laptops cost more?
stories.dek: AI data centres are absorbing the supply of memory chips, so gadget makers pay more for them. Apple says these costs will keep rising. Indian phone prices rose about 16% in early 2026.

so_far.text: Every phone, laptop and server needs two kinds of memory chip. DRAM is the working memory that holds what is open right now. NAND is the storage that keeps your photos and apps. Counterpoint Research, a market research firm, says AI data centres are now absorbing much of the DRAM and NAND supply. Memory has become more expensive as a result. In late June, Apple raised prices: the 14-inch MacBook Pro went up $300 and the iPad Air went up $150. In India, smartphone prices rose about 16% on average in the first half of 2026.

what_happened.text: Apple has released its fiscal fourth-quarter results. On its earnings call, where a company explains its quarterly results to investors, CEO John Ternus called the rise in memory prices "unprecedented". Reports published on 3 November quote him saying memory will cost Apple more in the December quarter, and that prices will keep rising after that. Digital Trends reads Apple's guidance as memory costs possibly pushing its gross margin down to 45–46%. CNET reports Ternus said the price rises and shortages will continue into 2027. CNET also reports the shortage may limit Mac and iPad supply over the holiday quarter.

steps.text: Phones, laptops and AI servers all use the same two memory types: DRAM for working memory and NAND for storage.
Counterpoint Research says AI data centres are absorbing much of that supply, so less is left for gadgets.
New memory factories take years to build, so device makers have to compete for a limited supply, and prices rise.
Makers then raise prices, as Apple did on Macs and iPads in June, or accept smaller profits.
In India a weaker rupee also makes imported parts dearer, which adds to the cost of making phones.

lesson.concept: How a dearer part squeezes a maker's margin
lesson.big_idea: Gross margin is the share of each sale a company keeps after paying to make the product. When a part like memory costs more, a maker must raise prices or accept a smaller margin.

steps.title: What gross margin means
steps.text: Gross margin is the share of each sale left after paying the direct cost of making the product. You work it out as sale price minus cost, divided by sale price.

steps.title: Memory is one slice of cost
steps.text: A phone or laptop's direct cost includes chips, screen, battery and assembly. Memory chips, DRAM and NAND, are one slice. Counterpoint Research says AI data centres are absorbing that supply, so memory costs more.

steps.title: Dearer parts shrink the margin
steps.text: If the sale price stays the same and memory costs more, the extra cost comes straight out of the margin. The company keeps less from every device it sells.

steps.title: Or the price must rise
steps.text: To keep the same margin, the maker must raise the price. Real makers often do some of both. Apple raised Mac and iPad prices in late June, and Lava is raising phone prices, citing memory costs.

example.setup: Say a laptop maker sells a laptop for ₹1,00,000. It costs ₹50,000 to make, including ₹10,000 of memory. Assume memory costs rise by half.

lines.label: Margin before
lines.note: Half of each sale is left after costs

lines.label: New memory cost
lines.note: Assume memory rises by half

lines.label: New total cost
lines.note: Only the memory cost changed

lines.label: Margin if price holds
lines.note: Five percentage points of margin are gone

lines.label: Price to keep 50%
lines.note: Cost must again be half the price

example.result: A rise in one part cut the margin from 50% to 45%. To protect the old margin, the price would have to rise 10%, from ₹1,00,000 to ₹1,10,000.

practice.q: A phone sells for ₹20,000 and costs ₹12,000 to make, including ₹2,000 of memory. Memory cost doubles. What is the new margin if the price stays the same?

options: It falls, because each sale leaves less after costs
It rises, because the memory inside is worth more
It stays the same, because the price did not change
check.why: Gross margin is price minus cost, as a share of price. A higher cost with the same price leaves a smaller share.

takeaways: When a part costs more, makers must raise prices or accept a smaller gross margin.
AI data centres are absorbing memory supply; Apple calls the price rise unprecedented and expects more.
Watch Lava's rise of up to ₹3,000 on 15 November; Counterpoint sees no fall before 2028.

sections.title: World
sections.gist: Russian strikes kill 31 in Ukraine before 10–11 November talks; South Africa's ANC faces a test; Poland guards its Kaliningrad border.

items.headline: Russian strike on Ukrainian aid shelter kills 31 before Abu Dhabi talks
items.text: On 2 November Russian strikes hit a shelter and a former school used as an aid site in Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region. AP reported on 3 November that the death toll had reached 31, with more than 45 residents missing. Overnight into 3 November, Russia launched 289 drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles. That is almost four drones for every missile. On 4 November Le Monde reported that Russia is stepping up strikes on civilian targets in Ukraine. Next: US-mediated peace talks are set for 10–11 November in Abu Dhabi.
items.background: The United States is mediating peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. The next round is set for Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November.
items.why: The deadly strikes on civilian sites come about one week before the next round of US-mediated peace talks.

items.headline: South Africa votes locally as ANC support expected to fall further
items.text: South Africans voted in local elections on 4 November. The vote is a tough test for the ANC, the African National Congress. In 2021 the party won under 50% in local elections, its first time since apartheid ended. In 2024 it lost its majority in parliament. It now leads a national unity government with the DA, the Democratic Alliance. The Guardian reports the ANC is expected to get less than a third of the vote. That would be a drop from under half to under a third. Voters are frustrated over water outages and power cuts. Results will show how far its support has fallen.
items.background: The ANC lost its parliamentary majority in 2024 and now shares national power with the DA in a unity government.
items.why: The results will show whether anger over water outages and power cuts keeps shrinking support for South Africa's main governing party.

items.headline: North Korea fires several missiles toward the East Sea
items.text: Early on 4 November North Korea fired multiple missiles toward the East Sea, the sea between Korea and Japan. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), its top military command, reported the launch. The missiles were fired from the Sondok area of South Hamgyong Province. The JCS believes they flew less than 300 km. The JCS gave no missile type. It said South Korea's military is watching North Korean activity closely. It also said it stays ready to respond overwhelmingly to any provocation. It is not yet known what kind of missiles were fired.
items.background: North Korea tests missiles from time to time. South Korea's military tracks each launch and reports its distance and direction.
items.why: No direct effect on India. South Korea's military says it is ready to respond overwhelmingly to any provocation.

items.headline: Poland sends special forces to Russian border after sabotage warnings
items.text: Poland has sent extra police, counterterrorism units and GROM special forces to two border regions, Warmia-Masuria and Podlaskie. These areas sit next to Kaliningrad, a piece of Russian territory between Poland and Lithuania. The operation began on Monday, 2 November, after intelligence warnings of sabotage. It runs until at least 8 November. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said people with flashlights were seen near the border overnight. He said Poland "successfully prevented any attempted acts of provocation, if that was the intention". He added that this can never be fully confirmed.
items.background: Poland is a NATO member bordering Russia's Kaliningrad, and tension with Russia has risen since the war in Ukraine began.
items.why: Any incident on a NATO border with Russia could widen the conflict in Europe.

items.headline: Indian tourist killed as two helicopters collide near Everest
items.text: On 3 November at about 8:11am local time, two helicopters collided while landing at a snowy helipad at Pheriche. Pheriche is in Nepal's Solukhumbu district, the Everest region. One helicopter belonged to Fishtail Air and the other to Air Dynasty. A 47-year-old Indian tourist was killed. A 49-year-old passenger from New Zealand and two Nepali pilots were injured. Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority has started an investigation. Its findings and timeline have not yet been announced.
items.background: Helicopters carry tourists and trekkers to high-altitude spots in the Everest region, where small, snowy helipads make landings difficult.
items.why: Many Indians travel to Nepal's mountains; the probe may show how safe these busy helicopter flights are.

sections.title: India
sections.gist: Supreme Court weighs immunity for election chiefs and leaves reserved-seat rotation to Parliament; blast hits a Rajasthan rail track; Cabinet funds minerals and energy storage.

items.headline: Blast damages Rajasthan railway track near Pakistan border
items.text: A blast damaged a railway track in Rajasthan near the Pakistan border, News18 and The Times of India reported on 4 November. Trains on the route were cancelled. Rajasthan's Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS), the state police's counter-terror unit, has started a probe. The Times of India reported that investigators are looking into a suspected plot to derail a train. No arrests or casualties were mentioned in the reports. It is not yet known who planted the explosive or why.
items.background: Rajasthan shares a long border with Pakistan, and its rail lines in that area carry both passengers and goods.
items.why: Rail travellers in western Rajasthan face cancellations, and an attempt to derail a train would be a serious security threat.

items.headline: Supreme Court questions poll officials' immunity; EC clarifies Form 6 re-enrolment
items.text: On 4 November the Supreme Court asked the Centre and the Election Commission to respond to a plea. The plea challenges the blanket immunity, or full legal protection, given to the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and Election Commissioners. Separately, the Election Commission said voters missing from the draft SIR voter lists can file Form 6. Form 6 is the form used to apply to join the voter list. The Election Commission said such voters will not face action, even if they were enrolled before. On 3 November, in a hearing on Delhi protests, the Supreme Court said no person or group can occupy a designated protest site indefinitely.
items.background: SIR is the Election Commission's revision of India's voter lists. A draft list has been published, and some voters are missing from it.
items.why: If your name is missing from the draft voter list, you can apply again using Form 6 without facing action.

items.headline: Supreme Court leaves rotation of SC/ST reserved seats to Parliament
items.text: On 4 November the Supreme Court rejected a plea asking it to order rotation of reserved constituencies. These are seats where only Scheduled Caste (SC) or Scheduled Tribe (ST) candidates can contest. Rotation would mean changing, from time to time, which seats are reserved. The court said this is for Parliament to decide, not the courts. So the current set of reserved seats stays as it is unless Parliament changes the law. It is not yet known whether Parliament will take up the question.
items.background: India reserves some Lok Sabha and Assembly seats for SC and ST candidates, so these communities are represented in law-making bodies.
items.why: The ruling decides who settles which seats are reserved, and that affects whom voters in those constituencies can elect.

items.headline: Cabinet clears ₹2,814 crore for minerals, ₹14,500 crore for storage
items.text: The Union Cabinet has approved two spending plans, reports on 4 November said. The first is ₹2,814 crore to support the processing of critical minerals. Critical minerals are raw materials, such as those used in batteries and electronics, that a country needs but may struggle to source. The second is ₹14,500 crore for energy storage, meaning systems that store electricity for later use. The storage plan is about five times the size of the minerals plan. Details on how and when the money will be paid out were not given in the reports.
items.background: India relies heavily on imports for many critical minerals, and needs storage to make solar and wind power usable when the sun or wind is absent.
items.why: The money aims to build Indian supply chains for batteries and clean power, which affect electricity reliability and costs.

sections.title: Your money & life
sections.gist: Cyclone Murasu left two dead and 312 houses damaged in Andhra Pradesh; relief work and alerts continue.

items.headline: Cyclone Murasu leaves two dead and 312 houses damaged in Andhra
items.text: Cyclone Murasu has left two people dead in Andhra Pradesh, The News Minute reported on 4 November. The storm also damaged 312 houses in the state. Each of those is a family whose home needs repair. The report gives figures only for Andhra Pradesh. It does not give figures for other states. It is not yet known whether the state government will announce compensation for families whose homes were damaged. Watch for official updates on the toll and on relief for affected households.
items.background: A cyclone is a large rotating storm that forms over warm sea water. Cyclone Murasu hit Andhra Pradesh.
items.why: Two deaths and 312 damaged homes show the cyclone's direct cost to families in Andhra Pradesh.

sections.title: Markets & money
sections.gist: India's services sector grew at a four-month high, gold jumped after the US midterms, and euro zone inflation reached 4%.

items.headline: India's services sector grows at four-month high in October
items.text: HSBC's India Services PMI rose to 55.8 in October, a four-month high, Mint reported on 4 November. A PMI is a monthly survey of companies. A reading above 50 means activity grew compared with the month before. So 55.8 means clear growth. Strong demand inside India drove the rise. Survey participants named new business as the main reason output grew. Cost pressures for service firms eased to a six-year low. But export orders and hiring slowed. It is not yet known whether the slower hiring will continue into November.
items.background: Services include work like banking, IT, hotels and transport. The PMI survey tracks them each month; above 50 means growth.
items.why: Easing costs can mean less pressure on service prices, but slower hiring is a caution for jobs.

items.headline: Company dollar hedging drops to eight-month low after RBI crackdown
items.text: Dollar hedging by Indian companies fell to an eight-month low after the RBI cracked down on rupee speculation, Business Standard reported on 4 November. Hedging works like this. A company that must pay dollars later locks in an exchange rate now. That protects it if the rupee weakens. Speculation is different: it is a bet placed to profit from the rupee's moves. The Hindu BusinessLine also reported the hedging slump. Separately, Reuters data published on 3 November showed the rupee's relative calm masks lingering anxiety. It is not yet known how long hedging will stay this low.
items.background: The RBI, India's central bank, has cracked down on speculative bets on the rupee, meaning trades made to profit from its moves.
items.why: How companies protect against a weaker rupee affects their costs, and Reuters data shows anxiety about the rupee remains.

items.headline: RBI sets up market advisory panel on liquidity and resilience
items.text: The RBI has set up a market advisory panel to address concerns about liquidity and resilience, Livemint reported on 4 November. Liquidity means how easily you can buy or sell something without moving its price much. In a liquid market, a big sale barely shifts the price. In a thin market, the same sale can push the price down sharply. Resilience means a market keeps working smoothly even under stress. The report does not name the panel's members. It is not yet known what the panel will recommend, or when.
items.background: The RBI, India's central bank, oversees key financial markets such as those for government bonds and currency.
items.why: Markets that stay liquid under stress help keep borrowing and trading smooth for banks, companies and savers.

items.headline: US stocks and gold rise, dollar and oil fall after midterms
items.text: US markets rose on 4 November after Democrats won control of Congress and President Trump said he would accept the results. At the open, the Dow rose about 1.8%, the S&P 500 about 1.1% and the Nasdaq about 1%, Al Jazeera reported. The dollar weakened. Gold surged about 3%, heading for its best day since August, as a cheaper dollar makes gold cheaper for buyers using other currencies. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell about 3.1% to roughly $100.40 a barrel. Markets often dislike uncertainty, and a clear result with an accepted outcome removed one source of it.
items.background: The US held midterm elections for Congress on 3 November. Democrats won both the Senate and the House.
items.why: Gold and crude prices feed directly into Indian jewellery prices, fuel costs and the import bill.

items.headline: Euro zone inflation hits 4% as race to replace Lagarde begins
items.text: Inflation in the euro zone reached 4%, its first time at that level in three years, CNBC reported on 4 November. An interest rate hike by the European Central Bank (ECB) now looms. The ECB is also choosing a new leader. Christine Lagarde is due to leave on 7 February 2027, nearly nine months before her eight-year term ends. Euro zone governments must nominate candidates by 6 November. Finance ministers will review them at the Eurogroup meeting on 9 November. So the next ECB chief may inherit a fight against rising prices from day one.
items.background: The ECB sets interest rates for the 20-plus countries that use the euro. Higher rates make borrowing costlier to slow price rises.
items.why: Europe is a major market for Indian exports. Higher rates there can slow demand and move global money flows.

items.headline: IEA warns Europe's gas stores could hit record lows after winter
items.text: The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned on 3 November that the EU's gas reserves could touch historic lows after the coming winter. Here is the chain. Europe fills its gas stores in summer and draws them down in winter for heating. If stores start winter low, they end winter even lower. Then Europe must buy more gas next year to refill them. That extra buying competes with other buyers worldwide. The IEA said these thin buffers could keep the global gas market tight well into 2027. How cold the winter turns out will decide how bad the shortfall gets.
items.background: The IEA is a Paris-based agency that tracks global energy supply. A 'tight' market means demand presses close to available supply, pushing prices up.
items.why: Gas is traded globally, so a tight market can raise costs for other buyers, including India.

sections.title: Tech & AI
sections.gist: AMD's strong results eased AI spending fears; Google will tie Search to AI for school accounts; scientists look to the new US Congress.

items.headline: AMD beats estimates as data-centre revenue nearly doubles
items.text: AMD's third-quarter earnings beat Wall Street estimates, Semafor reported on 3 November. Its data-centre revenue nearly doubled from a year earlier. Data centres are the large computer buildings that run AI and cloud services. So this figure tracks how much companies are spending on that computing. Before the results, a portfolio manager told Bloomberg that AMD needed not just a beat but a significant beat, with a strong outlook. AMD's shares rose after the results. It is not yet known whether other chipmakers will report similar growth.
items.background: Investors are testing whether the boom in spending on AI computing will continue. AMD sells chips used in data centres.
items.why: No direct effect on India. Data-centre chip sales are one signal of whether AI spending is still growing.

items.headline: Google to block Search for schools that switch off its AI
items.text: Google will turn off Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Search by default for K-12 student accounts, Gizmodo reported on 3 November. K-12 means school students from kindergarten to class 12. School administrators can switch these tools back on. But schools that disable AI entirely also lose Search. Students then see a message that search is unavailable. Google's Chris Phillips said "Search and A.I. are deeply integrated." Google says it will share more details in the coming months before the changes roll out. It plans to test Guided Learning in Search at select US schools later in November 2026.
items.background: Google's tools are widely used by schools through student accounts. Many schools are unsure whether to allow AI tools for children.
items.why: Schools may no longer be able to keep Google Search while saying no to AI. Whether this applies outside the US is not stated.

items.headline: Scientists hope Democratic Congress will push back on Trump science policy
items.text: Democrats took control of Congress in the 3 November midterm elections, after a crushing defeat for President Trump's Republicans, DW reported. Researchers now hope lawmakers will push back against the Trump administration's science policies, the journal Nature reported on 4 November. But Nature also notes there are limits to what Congress can do. Here is why. Congress writes laws and approves budgets. The president's administration runs the agencies that spend the money and carry out policy. So a Congress controlled by the other party can block or reshape plans, but cannot run the agencies itself. How far Democrats will go is not yet known.
items.background: The US Congress has two chambers, the Senate and the House. Laws and federal budgets need both to pass them.
items.why: US science funding shapes global research, including work and collaborations involving Indian scientists and students.

sections.title: Science, health & climate
sections.gist: WHO adds two Ebola vaccine candidates to the trial in Congo, while India's first dengue vaccine, QDENGA, is due in early 2027.

items.headline: India's first dengue vaccine, QDENGA, is due in early 2027
items.text: Takeda's dengue vaccine QDENGA got marketing approval in July 2026 from the CDSCO, India's drug regulator. The approval covers people aged 4 to 60, so both children and adults can get it. The vaccine is expected in India in the first half of 2027. It would be the country's first dengue vaccine. On 4 November India Today reported that an earlier dengue vaccine, Dengvaxia, still casts a shadow over the launch. That earlier vaccine had safety problems. It is not yet known how these concerns will affect who gets QDENGA, or how quickly it is taken up.
items.background: Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease. An earlier vaccine against it, Dengvaxia, ran into safety problems that experts still remember.
items.why: QDENGA would give Indians aged 4 to 60 their first vaccine option against dengue, from the first half of 2027.

items.headline: Two new vaccines join Ebola trial in DR Congo
items.text: On 4 November the WHO said two new candidate vaccines will join the Tumaini trial in DR Congo. They are ChAdOx1 from Oxford and the Serum Institute, and mRNA-1469 from Moderna. Both target the Bundibugyo virus and joined after national approvals. Tumaini is a ring-vaccination trial. That means vaccinating the contacts of each patient, and their contacts, to build a ring of protection. A separate WHO treatment trial, PARTNERS, began in July. It tests the antibody MBP134 and the drug remdesivir, alone or together. Maftivimab will be added soon. First findings are expected in the coming months.
items.background: An Ebola outbreak in DR Congo is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, one type of Ebola virus.
items.why: One candidate vaccine involves the Serum Institute, the Indian vaccine maker, and the trials test tools against this outbreak.

sections.title: Formula 1
sections.gist: Cadillac F1's owner weighs a partial sale at a $3bn valuation, while Mercedes, Honda and Ferrari sort through what went wrong in Mexico.

items.headline: Cadillac F1 owner TWG weighs partial sale at $3bn valuation
items.text: On 4 November Autosport, citing Sportico, reported that TWG Global is looking to sell part of its majority stake in the Cadillac F1 team. TWG is led by Mark Walter. The deal would value the whole team at around $3bn. Fenway Sports Group, which owns Liverpool FC and baseball's Red Sox, is reportedly among several interested buyers. TWG at first dismissed suggestions of a sale. GM declined to comment. The reports have raised fresh doubts about who will own the majority of the team. It is not yet known whether any sale will happen, or how big a share would change hands.
items.background: Cadillac F1 is majority-owned by Mark Walter's TWG Global. Carmaker GM, which owns the Cadillac brand, is also linked to the team.
items.why: A team's owners set its budget and direction. A $3bn price tag also shows what investors now think an F1 team is worth.

items.headline: Mexico GP fallout: Mercedes admits fault, Honda explains, Ferrari teammates clash
items.text: After the Mexico Grand Prix, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff admitted the team 'let down' George Russell. An energy deployment problem dropped Russell from the front row to sixth by Turn 1. Honda said Mexico City's altitude put its ERS cooling circuit under more stress than expected. The ERS stores electrical energy and releases it as extra power. That forced Aston Martin's early retirements. Thin air also worsened turbo lag, the delay before the turbo delivers power, because there is no MGU-H. At Ferrari, Charles Leclerc got a five-second penalty for clashing with Lewis Hamilton. Nico Rosberg blamed Leclerc. Le Parisien reports Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur was angry.
items.background: Mexico City sits at high altitude. The thin air there puts extra strain on engines, cooling and turbochargers.
items.why: Mexico showed how energy and cooling problems can wreck a team's race in its first laps.

sections.title: Cricket — the masala
sections.gist: Kohli and young pacers put India 1-0 up in New Zealand, and the WPL 2027 dates and venues are announced.

items.headline: Kohli's 51 and young pacers put India 1-0 up in New Zealand
items.text: India beat New Zealand in the rain-hit first ODI in Auckland on 4 November. India chose to bowl and picked fast bowlers Auqib Nabi and Anshul Kamboj in the XI. New Zealand were bowled out for 185. Rain then cut India's chase to a revised target of 143. India reached it in 22.4 overs. Virat Kohli's 51 off 51 balls did most of the work. Kamboj took 2 for 22, exactly a month after an expensive ODI debut. He said one bad match doesn't affect him. New Zealand's Tim Seifert made his ODI comeback. India now lead the five-match series 1-0, with four games left.
items.background: When rain cuts playing time, a formula gives the chasing side fewer overs and a lower target, so both sides get a fair contest.
items.why: Kamboj's strong second match after a costly debut gives India's young pace attack more confidence for the rest of the series.

items.headline: WPL 2027 to run 14 January–7 February in Vadodara and Mumbai
items.text: On 4 November the BCCI released the schedule for the fifth Women's Premier League (WPL). It runs from 14 January to 7 February 2027. Defending champions RCB face MI in the opening match. Vadodara will host the first 11 league matches. The other nine league games move to Mumbai's Brabourne Stadium. The knockouts will also be played at the Brabourne. So only two cities will host all 20 league matches and the knockouts, across about three and a half weeks.
items.background: The WPL is the BCCI's franchise league for women cricketers. The 2027 season is its fifth edition.
items.why: Fans in Vadodara and Mumbai get every WPL 2027 game nearby. Everyone else can now plan travel or viewing around fixed dates.

quiz.q: Democrats pass a bill through both houses by simple majorities, and Trump vetoes it. What happens next?
options: It becomes law anyway, because Democrats control Congress
It dies unless two-thirds of both houses vote to override
The Vice President casts the deciding vote
quiz.why: A majority can pass a bill, but only two-thirds of both houses can override a veto. That needs Republican votes.

quiz.q: Trump says aid to Israel ends by year-end. Why could the money still flow?
options: Because Israel has refused to accept the cut
Because the aid levels are in US law and Congress controls yearly funding
Because the 2016 MOU legally binds the president
quiz.why: MOUs are not binding, but Congress wrote the levels into a 2021 law and releases money each year through appropriations.

quiz.q: Gulf oil exports fell in October, yet Brent dropped 8.6% on 4 November. What best explains this?
options: Hormuz reopened and tankers returned
Traders saw better odds of a deal, shrinking the war risk premium
Iran accepted all US conditions
quiz.why: Supply had not recovered. The price fell because future disruption looked less likely after the US election result.
